newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Desperate Albanians clash with police in port city.
newsitem.headline: Desperate Albanians clash with police in port city.

text.p: Fresh violence erupted at the Albanian port of Durres on Sunday as about 3,000 Albanians chanting "Peace, peace" gathered in Tirana's central square as part of government attempts to restore order.
European Union foreign ministers agreed to send military and police advisers to Albania but said they would not mount a military operation to end the violence that has gripped the Balkan country.

President Sali Berisha, facing mounting criticism since the collapse of shady investment schemes into which thousands of Albanians had poured their savings, defied demands from southern rebels that he should quit.

Celebratory gunfire erupted in the southern rebel stronghold of Gjirokaster on Saturday night when rumours that Berisha had quit circulated. The guns were fired again, this time in anger, when the resignation was officially denied.
In Durres, 30 km (20 miles) west of the capital Tirana, scores of Albanian police clashed with about a thousand civilians trying to flee the country, witnesses said.
The police beat some civilians and fired hundreds of Kalashnikov rounds over their heads to drive them back from the gates of Albania's largest port.
"We are not killing the people, because they are our brothers, but we have to guard the port," explained one harassed policeman.
"The people are coming here because they hope to go to Italy but there is no ship for them."
In Tirana, the government had declared Sunday a day of mourning for the more than 100 people killed, mostly by stray bullets.
Police aboard vans and a single armoured vehicle manned by gun-toting security men patrolled Skanderbeg Square as the crowd clapped their hands, sang patriotic songs and staged a brief march.
Some chanted "Hand in the Arms," a reference to appeals for gunmen who have been rampaging through Albanian towns to give up their weapons.
Albania's flag, a double-headed black eagle on a red background, stood at half mast by a mounted statue of 15th century national hero Gjergj Kastriot Skanderbeg.
The government has sought to restore order by parading armoured vehicles and tanks through the streets of Tirana, increasing police pay and issuing repeated appeals for an end to the violence.

Unrest erupted across southern Albania in January over the collapse of fraudulent pyramid investment schemes. It spread to most of the country in recent weeks, turning into a lawless revolt against Berisha.
At least 20 people have died in Tirana during two days of shooting this week.
The European Union, divided over what to do about Albania, agreed on Sunday to send military and police advisers in a bid to help restore order.
EU foreign ministers meeting in The Netherlands also agreed to consider providing protection for this mission if necessary, but stressed this was not a military operation.
"Any interventionist approach is off the table," one German diplomatic source said. Sharp divisions over the question of military intervention had emerged at the meeting on Saturday.

The EU said in a communique it was "strongly committed to helping Albania restore civilian structures and law and order", adding that outside help was needed immediately to restore security, in particular in and around Tirana.
Meanwhile, the exodus of Albanians across the Adriatic Sea to Italy showed no sign of easing off.
Italian coastguards said they had rescued 858 Albanian refugees, including a heavily pregnant woman and a new-born baby, from a ship that ran aground off the port of Brindisi.
Another 317 fleeing Albanians arrived during the night at the larger Italian port of Bari further to the north on three fishing boats.
Pope John Paul urged Albanians to end "destructive violence" and lay down their arms and said the whole of Europe had a duty to help rebuild the country.

"For the good of Albania, I urge all those who have taken up arms to lay them down. Destructive violence is definitely not the right way to resolve social problems," the Pontiff said in a regular weekly address to pilgrims in St Peter's Square.
